content.thinking:
I'm putting together the postmortem and have the key timeline in view. The monthly-spend-feature flag was turned on at 15:47:53 by an admin, and ZeroDivisionError errors at spend_summary.py:47 started right after. Switching the flag off at 15:54:14 didn't clear the incident by 15:56:00, so I'm now checking why the flag was put back on at 15:57:03.

I'm checking whether the flag change actually reached the service, since the errors kept going after it was switched off, and I'm weighing whether the revert really was refuted or whether something else is going on.

I'm weighing whether the flag is really the trigger, since switching it off by 15:56 didn't clear the errors. The record doesn't show whether that switch-off ever reached the service, so the link between the flag and the failures isn't settled yet.

I'm ruling out an earlier deployment, since the record shows only the flag change went out in the day before onset and every replica runs one revision. The flag was off before 15:47 while the service looked healthy, so the earlier state doesn't explain the failures.

I'm listing out the chain of causes now, starting from the failing account pages and tracing each step back to the flag and the code at spend_summary.py:47.

I'm tying the failing account pages to the ZeroDivisionError at spend_summary.py:47, which divides the month's total by the count of this-month purchases and so fails for shoppers who bought before but not this month. I'm also noting that the flag went to every request at once, with no staged rollout visible, which is a contributing factor in how the change got through.

I'm now listing the two contributing factors: the flag went from off to on for every evaluation at once with no staged rollout, and no check was seen that runs the flag-on path before the flag goes on in production.

I'm adding the contributing factors: no check was seen before the flag went on, and nobody was paged when the alert fired, so I'm planning an on-call routing item for the high error rate alert.

I'm weighing whether the flag switch-off actually reached the service, since the logs stop at 15:54 and the errors kept going. After the revert, the flag went back on at 15:57, so the trigger is in production again while the failures continue, and I'm noting that the response left it there as designed. I'm treating the revert as a failed mitigation, which left the incident without a working fix when Argus escalated.

I'm weighing whether to call the revert a failed mitigation, since the second investigation landed on the same refuted flag cause without offering anything new. The judgement window was only about a minute after the switch-off, so I'm also wondering whether that was too short to read the outcome.

I'm checking whether the revert was ever really tested, since the record only shows the flag going back on at 15:57 and the failures continuing. Switching the flag off doesn't seem to have stopped the harm, and I'm not yet sure what would.

I'm now deciding what to do about the flag, since switching it off hasn't stopped the errors. I'd switch monthly-spend-feature off again and keep it off, then confirm at io-shop that its evaluation log lines read off for every request and that the ZeroDivisionError lines at spend_summary.py:47 stop.

I'm now deciding what to try next for the "why" question: I want to read io-shop's flag evaluation log lines after the switch-off to see whether they actually came back off, and if they did, find what else is reaching the division at spend_summary.py:47. I'm also starting on the action items, and I'm leaning toward a staged rollout for flag changes on io-shop as the first prevention item.

I'm settling on the action items now: a staged rollout to limit how many shoppers a flag change reaches at once, a CI test that runs the flag-on path before a flag can go on in production, and paging the on-call engineer when the high error rate alert fires. I'm also thinking about what still puts account pages at risk while the flag stays on.

I'm now writing the root cause in plain terms: with monthly-spend-feature on, the spend summary divides the month's total by the count of this month's purchases, so it fails for shoppers who have bought before but nothing this month.

I'm now settling on how to phrase the root cause and the symptom. The timestamp of the flag change goes into the chain, and I'm checking the step where the flag routes requests to the spend summary path. I'm also deciding whether to cite the flag change as the mechanism, and then I'll look at what else I still need to rule out.

I'm ruling out a deployment as the cause, since the change events for the day before onset show only the flag change and every replica runs the same revision. With the flag off, account pages rendered normally and the error rate stayed near its usual level, so that earlier state doesn't explain the failures.

I'm checking the assumptions behind the timeline, mainly that the failing account pages are the 5xx requests in the alert series, which the error rates support. I'm also treating the ZeroDivisionError lines as the failing requests behind that series. Next I'm turning to the mitigation agent's switch of the flag and whether it was timed properly.

I'm now going through the remaining items: the switch-off, the checks on the flag evaluation logs, and which parts of the record I should cite as already settled.

action_items.item: Make flag changes on io-shop roll out to a small share of traffic first, and widen them only while the account page error rate stays at its usual level.
Require a test that runs the code path an io-shop flag turns on, including for shoppers with no purchases this month, and have it pass before the flag can be switched on in production.
Route the HighErrorRate alert on io-shop to page the on-call engineer.

causal_chain.step: Shoppers' account page requests failed, and the share of failed account page requests in the minute rose far above its usual level.
The failing account page requests raised ZeroDivisionError (division by zero) at src/io_shop/spend_summary.py:47. These errors started in the minute of the onset and were not seen before it.

ruled_out.what: A deploy or release: the change events read for the day before the onset held only this flag change, and every replica ran one revision.
The service with the flag off: before the onset every evaluation read off, account pages rendered normally, and the error rate was typically low.
Shoppers closing the connection: these ClientDisconnected failures were already being logged during the healthy stretch before the onset, while the error rate stayed typically low.

causal_chain.step: An admin switched the feature flag monthly-spend-feature on at {P1.1}. Flag evaluations went from all off to all on starting in that minute, so account page requests began running the spend summary code path that the flag turns on.
The spend summary path divides by the number of purchases made this month, and that number is zero for a shopper who has bought before but not this month.

input.cause_in_plain_words: Account pages started failing when a setting switched on a new monthly spending summary, and that summary likely breaks for shoppers who have bought before but nothing this month, because it divides by the number of this month's purchases.

contributing_factors.factor: monthly-spend-feature went from off to on for every evaluation at once. No staged rollout to a small share of traffic was seen.
contributing_factors.had_it_been_otherwise: Only a small share of account page requests would have taken the failing path, and the errors could have been caught before the flag reached all traffic.
contributing_factors.label: CF-1

contributing_factors.factor: Before the flag was switched on in production, no check was seen that ran the code path it turns on for a shopper with past purchases but none this month.
contributing_factors.had_it_been_otherwise: The division by zero would have shown up before the flag went on, and the flag would not have been switched on with the path failing.
contributing_factors.label: CF-2

contributing_factors.factor: Nobody was paged: HighErrorRate on io-shop was not linked to any on-call incident.
contributing_factors.had_it_been_otherwise: A person would have been working the incident from the alert onward, including after the flag revert did not help, rather than only when a draft pull request was left for review.
contributing_factors.label: CF-3

went_well.item: The Investigator Agent placed the start of the incident in the minute the flag was switched on.
The Investigator Agent tied the failures to the ZeroDivisionError at src/io_shop/spend_summary.py:47 and the flag change in candidate C1.
The Mitigation Agent switched monthly-spend-feature off for C1, a change that can be put back.
The Code-Fix Agent proposed a fix as draft pull request #575 for a person to review.

went_wrong: Switching off the flag that the onset lines up with did not take the service off the incident's level. That left the incident with no mitigation, and the service was still failing when Argus escalated.
The second investigation formed C2, which blames the same flag move that had just been tested and refuted, so it offered nothing new to try.

input.root_cause: With monthly-spend-feature on, `render_spend_summary` sends the account page request to `average_spend_per_item_this_month`, which divides the month's total spend by the number of purchases flagged `in_current_month`. For a shopper who has bought before but not this month that number is zero, so the request raises ZeroDivisionError at src/io_shop/spend_summary.py:47 and the account page fails.
input.still_at_risk: Account page requests could go on failing with the division-by-zero error at src/io_shop/spend_summary.py:47 while monthly-spend-feature stays on, and it was left on.
input.stops_the_harm: Switch monthly-spend-feature off again. Confirm at io-shop that its flag evaluation log lines read off for every evaluation and that the ZeroDivisionError lines at src/io_shop/spend_summary.py:47 stop.
input.why_it_did_not_help: Find out from io-shop's flag evaluation log lines after the switch-off whether the service read monthly-spend-feature as off. If it did, find out what else kept reaching the division at src/io_shop/spend_summary.py:47 and kept the account pages failing.
